newsitem.title: UK: Dlr calmer in Europe on soothing words from Japan.
newsitem.headline: Dlr calmer in Europe on soothing words from Japan.

text.p: The dollar opened slightly firmer in Europe against the yen and the mark, helped by more soothing comments from Japanese officials overnight in the wake of recent wild market swings.
The dollar regained a foothold above Friday's session low at 119 yen having dipped to lowest level in almost four-months on Monday at 117.50.

"A raft of comments from Japanese officials helped stabilise the situation and I think they were genuinely taken aback by the sheer speed of the dollar's fall since last week," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.

Japanese ministry of finance officials precipitated the biggest one-week dollar/yen decline since 1989 last week by warning the markets about possible intervention to prevent further yen weakness. This combined with growing talk of a Japanese interest rate rise to send the dollar into tailspin.
Earlier today, however, Japan's finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee he expects foreign exchange markets to settle down soon at an appropriate level.
Bank of Japan director Yatuka Yamaguchi, meantime, said it was important for foreign exchange rates to stabilise at levels reflecting economic fundamentals.

At 0750 GMT, the dollar was trading at 119.20/30 yen compared with 118.67/77 late Monday. Against the mark, it was little changed from Monday just above the psychological 1.70 level at 1.7005/10 compared with 1.7010/20 late yesterday.
Traders said the mark/yen rate, which slumped to its lowest level in almost a year yesterday, was key to watch for further yen moves having also bounced sharply late Monday.

Speculation about a possible rise in Japanese interest rates continued to bubble and this will underpin the yen's recent gains, traders said. Rising bond yields show how the market is moving to discount a rate rise in the months ahead, they said.

Hawkins at Bank of America said the Industrial Bank of Japan's decision Monday to raise its long-term prime rate to 3.1 percent from 2.5 percent, effective May 14, underscored the pressure on interest rates. Other major banks followed today.

News of a 12.7 percent drop in Japanese machinery orders in March tempered this view overnight but Japan's Economic Planning Agency said it expects machine orders to be up 4.5 percent for the whole April-to-June quarter and the trend was rising.
Japanese industry appears happy with the dollar retreat, meantime, and Toyota Motor Corp chairman Shoichiro Toyoda said earlier that a range of 110-to-120 was appropriate.
Elsewhere, there was little impact from news final German consumer price data from April showed a drop in the annual inflation rate to 1.4 percent from 1.5 percent in March.

Traders awaited the release of the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report at 1030 GMT. Sterling eased a touch against the mark ahead of the report amid expectations the central bank will be more upbeat about the chances of meeting the UK's 2.5 percent inflation target and thus easing pressure for another immediate rise in interest rates.
"With the Bank of England now independent this report will become more and more important," said a trader at a UK bank.
The U.S. April retail sales report is due out at 1230 GMT.

Analysts polled by Reuters expect a drop of 0.3 percent during the month and this is expected to throw more cold water on expectations of a U.S. interest rate rise next week. This could limit the extent of any dollar recovery today, traders said.
